In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in order to detect the gravitons of quintessential inflationary scenarios, the sensitivity of the detectors should be improved by at least two orders of magnitude.

, in the case of a blue spectrum, the sensitivity to the relic gravitonic signal can be significantly enhanced by using the same detector twice, with the second measurement being made with the detector rotated by 90$^o$.
the sensitivity of interferometers depends on the shape of the spectrum of the signal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, if we assume the same noise power spectral densities, the sensitivities of wide band detectors are higher in the case of violet gravitons.
, for blue spectra, the sensitivities of LIGO and VIRGO detectors are comparable, and that the sensitivities of VIRGO-LIGO and LISA-Virgo-LIGO pairs of detectors are similar.

, in the class of models considered in the paper, the sensitivity of wide band interferometric detectors to the relic gravittons is always better than the sensitivity of narrow band resonant detectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sensitivities to blue spectra of relic gravtions are always larger that the corresponding sensitivities to violet spectra.

, in the case of blue spectra, the signal-to-noize ratio is not a monotonic function of the energy, and therefore the sensitivity to $h_{0}^2 \Omega_{GW} $ cannot be computed simply by taking the ratio between the noise spectral energy density and the signal spectral energy density.

the sensitivity of the interferometric gravitational wave detectors is not only determined by the noise power spectral density of the detectors but it depends also upon the spectral shape of the signal.
